overview: Kaqchikel communities belong to Guatemala’s Maya world. Before Spanish invasion, Iximche headed a powerful western confederation, while eastern Chajoma’ communities retained substantial independence. The imported 1492-1500 outline is a broad cultural approximation, not proof that Iximche governed every place inside it. This account follows the capital’s archaeology and later Kaqchikel writing, family life and learning.

sections.title: A capital built for politics and ordinary meals

items.text: Iximche was founded between 1463 and 1470 after a break with K’iche’ power. Its ruling alliance included the Xajil and Sotz’il groups. A rebellion by the Tuquche’ in 1493 reveals sharp disagreements within the confederation, rather than a single harmonious royal household.

The capital occupied a defensible ridge with steep ravines. Yet archaeological discussion also places settlement beyond its fortified core. Looking only at the surviving plazas would leave much of the lived-in town outside the picture.

Excavators found built-in benches and sunken hearths in the Great Palace. Grinding stones, obsidian knives, tortilla griddles and kitchen vessels lay among its remains. Even an impressive palace needed equipment for the unglamorous daily business of making dinner.

The builders levelled plazas on sloping ground and installed cement-lined gutters to carry rainwater away. Managing a downpour was part of urban engineering. These excavated channels document drainage; the report does not identify them as toilets.

Structure 8 was a ballcourt with a playing area about 100 feet long and 23 feet wide. Two coats of plaster preserved evidence of renovation. Keeping a public playing surface usable was a recurring construction job.

Temple 2 once had painted decoration in red, yellow and blue. Fine incised outlines helped guide the painted figures. The surviving fragments remind us that buildings now seen as subdued ruins could originally carry vivid color.

Spanish forces initially entered Iximche as allies in 1524. Abusive tribute demands helped turn alliance into resistance, and Kaqchikel leaders abandoned the city. The struggle continued beyond the capital’s evacuation, with resistance documented at least through 1535.

sections.title: Family records, weaving and a language still used

items.text: A manuscript now at Penn Libraries includes births, baptisms, marriages, disputes and community contributions dated between 1586 and 1619. Its family record was also a civic record: remembering who married or contributed could matter alongside remembering rulers and wars.

The surviving manuscript was probably copied between 1619 and 1650 and contains 50 paper leaves, written in indigo ink. Several Xahila-family writers contributed to its history. Its present form is a colonial-era witness carrying memories of earlier generations.

A short written sample is “Haok ki xoh pax pa tinamit vae.” Brinton’s 1885 edition translates its heading as “How We went forth from the City.” It introduces the account of leaving Iximche. This preserves that edition’s spelling, rather than modern standardized Kaqchikel.

For a 2008 exhibition, Spurlock Museum displayed three Kaqchikel women’s blouses, or po’t, made on backstrap looms. Their designs represented particular towns. Magda Silvia Sotz Mux served as cultural consultant and guest artist, helping visitors understand clothing through a maker’s knowledge.

A health project reported in 2020 worked with midwives to improve a newborn-care phone application. Pictograms and Kaqchikel audio prompts reduced dependence on typed text. Midwives tested changes with the developers, contributing practical expertise about how the tool would work during actual visits.

Oxlajuj Aj, Tulane’s Kaqchikel language program in Guatemala, began in 1987. Expert local instructors combine spoken practice with grammar and writing, while local leaders and scholars give presentations. Students learn by using the language, including structured practice that avoids translating every sentence through Spanish or English.

ending.text: The map’s 1500 cutoff is not an ending. Iximche lost its role during Spanish invasion, but Kaqchikel communities continued recording history and family affairs; Kaqchikel remains a language of teaching and daily expertise.
